newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Stark vows to meet tough EMU goals.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Stark vows to meet tough EMU goals.

text.p: German State Secretary in the Finance Ministry Juergen Stark said on Thursday the Maastricht criteria for entry into the European single currency must be strictly adhered to, adding there was no doubt Germany would meet these goals.

Stark also sought to calm market concern about the renewed rise in the dollar against the German currency, saying that a dollar/mark exchange rate of over 1.72 marks was part of a normal correction in foreign exchange markets.

Stark, speaking at a breakfast meeting hosted by a local group of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, insisted the economic criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU) could not be departed from.
"The criteria were not anchored in the Maastricht Treaty only for us then to depart from them. We want to take them seriously and we must take them seriously," he said.

His comments follow the traditional German hard-line interpretation of the treaty but come as Bonn itself appears to be having trouble fulfilling the prerequisites for EMU entry, particularly the rule limiting the annual state budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product.
But Stark insisted: "We shall meet the deficit criterion. There is no doubt about that...I don't know where this doubt is coming from."

Some independent economists have expressed doubt that Germany would meet the deficit target range, particularly as it was still struggling with stubbornly high unemployment rates, costing the government considerable funds.

But Stark said there was no need for the German government to alter its 1997 budget deficit forecast after March jobs numbers, which showed only a 15,000 fall in unemployment to a seasonally adjusted 4.30 million in March.

"(Our deficit forecast) remains in place after the latest labour market data," Stark said, referring to the government's forecast that Germany's budget deficit will total 2.9 percent of gross domestic product in 1997.
Stark added that the EMU project had been formulated with agreements on rules, regulations and obligations "to ensure that the euro currency will be a stable currency."
He said that as a result he saw no reason for an automatic dollar appreciation due to the introduction of the new money.
On the German currency, Stark said the recent climb of the dollar to around 1.72 marks was a "normal correction" on foreign exchange markets.
The mark, which touched a 37-month low in overnight foreign exchange trade at 1.7272, later firmed slightly to trade at 1.7173 against the dollar by midday in Europe trading.
